'''''Lycium barbarum''''' is a [[shrub]] native to China,<ref Name=grin/><ref Name=aussie2/><ref Name=floraweb/> with present-day range across Asia and southeast Europe.<ref>{{cite book |first1=Harrison Leigh |last1=Flint |chapter=''Lycium barbarum'' |chapter-url = https://books.google.com/books?id=Q1_fAywb_bkC&pg=PA326 |title=Landscape plants for eastern North America: exclusive of Florida and the immediate Gulf Coast |publisher=John Wiley & Sons |location=Chichester |year=1997 |page=326 |isbn=978-0-471-59919-7}}</ref> It is one of two species of [[boxthorn]] in the family [[Solanaceae]] from which the [[goji]] berry or wolfberry is harvested, the other being ''[[Lycium chinense]]''.

Common names of the plant in [[English language|English]] include '''Chinese wolfberry''',<ref name=grin>{{GRIN | accessdate = 22 December 2017}}</ref> '''barbary matrimony vine''',<ref name=grin/>  '''red medlar'''<ref>{{cite web |url = https://www.telegraph.co.uk/gardening/3344996/Goji-berries-The-new-superfruit.html|title=Goji berries: The new superfruit|publisher=The Telegraph, Telegraph Media Group Limited, London, UK|date=12 October 2007|author=McAdam, Diana}}</ref> or '''matrimony vine'''.<ref name=grin/>  In the [[United Kingdom]] it is also known as '''Duke of Argyll's tea tree''' after [[Archibald Campbell, 3rd Duke of Argyll]] who introduced it in the country in the 1730s.<ref Name=grin/>

The shrub is an important commercial crop in northern China, especially in the [[Ningxia]] [[Hui people|Hui]] [[Autonomous regions of China|Autonomous Region]].  Its [[Chinese language|Chinese]] name is ''Ningxia gǒuqǐ''.

== Description ==
[[File:Illustration Lycium barbarum0.jpg|right|thumb|''Lycium barbarum'' illustration from ''Flora von Deutschland, Österreich und der Schweiz'', by Prof. Dr. Otto Wilhelm Thomé, 1885, Gera, Germany.]]

''Lycium barbarum'' is a [[deciduous]] [[wood]]y shrub that typically grows to a height of {{convert|1|–|3|m}}. It is characterised by its weak arching branches, and the side branches are often reduced to short leafless spines.<ref name=aussie2>Government of South Australia (2007), "[http://www.flora.sa.gov.au/efsa/lucid/Solanaceae/Solanaceae%20species/key/Australian%20Solanaceae%20species/Media/Html/Lycium_barbarum.htm ''Lycium barbarum'']". Online fact sheet on ''Electronic Flora of South Australia'' (''eFloraSA''). Accessed on 2018-05-04.</ref>

=== Leaves and flowers ===
[[File:Lycium barbarum Flower Closeup Miguelturra CampodeCalatrava.jpg|thumb|left|230px|''L. barbarum'' leaves and flower]]

''L. barbarum'' leaves form on the shoot either in an alternating arrangement, or in bundles of up to three.  Each leaf is green, scarcely fleshy when fresh, usually [[lanceolate]] (spearhead-shaped), sometimes with rounded tips.<ref name=floraweb>T. Muer (2000), "[http://www.floraweb.de/pflanzenarten/foto.xsql?suchnr=3555 ''Lycium Barabarum'']".  Image on the ''Floraweb'' website, from "Bildatlas der Farn- und Blütenpflanzen Deutschlands" by H. Haeupler and T. Muer, 2000. Accessed on 2018-05-04.</ref> Clustered leaves are up to 25 mm long; the single alternate leaves are up to 55 mm long.<ref name=aussie2/>

The flowers grow in groups of one to three in the leaf [[axil]]s, with [[pedicel (botany)|pedicel]]s 6–15 mm long. The [[sepal|calyx]], eventually ruptured by the growing berry, is a whitish tube crowned by five or six radial triangular [[sepals]], shorter than the tube, 10–12 mm long and 3–4 mm wide, sometimes 2–lipped, strongly curved.  The sepals are whitish on the lower side (facing towards the branch) and deep mauve on the top side.  Each flower has five stamens, exserted for 3–8 mm, with stalks longer than the [[anther]]s.<ref name=aussie2/>   The [[pistil]] is 8–11.5 mm long.  The anthers are longitudinally [[dehiscence (botany)|dehiscent]].{{citation needed|date=May 2018}}

=== Fruit ===
The fruit of ''L. barbarum'', the main variety of [[goji|goji berry]], is a bright orange-red, [[ellipsoid]] berry {{convert|1-2|cm|in|abbr=on}} in diameter.  The fruiting [[calyx (flower)|calyx]] is split deeply once or twice.  The number of seeds in each berry varies widely based on [[cultivar]] and fruit size, ranging from 10 to 60.  The seeds are about 2 mm long, 1 mm wide, yellowish, compressed with a curved embryo.

===Reproduction===
The plants are self-pollinating, but may be cross pollinated by insects.{{citation needed|date=May 2018}}  The species is dispersed into natural areas by birds and other animals that eat its fruit.<ref name=aussie1/>

In the Northern Hemisphere, flowering occurs from June through September and berry maturation from August to October, depending on the latitude, altitude, and climate.  Where frost does not occur fruiting is continuous and plants do not lose their leaves.{{citation needed|date=May 2018}}

==Occurrence and cultivation==

===China===
''Lycium barbarum'' has been cultivated in China, along the fertile aggradational [[floodplains]] of the [[Yellow River]], for more than 600 years. It is still extensively cultivated in the [[Ningxia Hui Autonomous Region]] of [[Northwestern China|north-central China]], centered in [[Zhongning County]], totaling 200,000 acres as of 2005,<ref name="xinhua05">[https://translate.google.com/translate?u=http%3A%2F%2Fwww.nx.xinhuanet.com%2F20050713%2Fgq.htm&hl=en&ie=UTF-8&sl=zh-CN&tl=en] Xinhua News Agency, Opening ceremonies of Ningxia wolfberry festival, August 3, 2005.</ref>  The region produced 13,000 tons of fruit in 2001, accounting for 42% of the nation's total production of goji berries. The plant is also cultivated in the [[Xinjiang|Xinjiang Uyghur Autonomous Region]] of [[western China]],<!-- Is this L barbarum or L. chinensis?-->

The berries of ''L. barbarum'' are the only therapeutic grade ("superior-grade") kinds of wolfberries used by practitioners of traditional Chinese medicine.<ref>[http://english.people.com.cn/english/200108/19/eng20010819_77685.html] Staff reporter, China's first provincial-level wolfberry association established, People's Daily Online, August 19, 2001.</ref>

As Ningxia's borders merge with three [[desert]]s, ''L. barbarum'' is also planted to control [[erosion]] and reclaim irrigable soils from [[desertification]].<ref>[http://www.bjreview.com.cn/nation/txt/2008-10/11/content_156256.htm] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150923191508/http://www.bjreview.com.cn/nation/txt/2008-10/11/content_156256.htm |date=2015-09-23 }} Yunyun L. Dry no more. BeijingReview.com.cn, October 11, 2008.</ref>

===United Kingdom===
''Lycium barbarum'' has been used since the 18th century in the [[United Kingdom]] for hedging, especially in coastal districts. Its red berries are attractive to a wide variety of British birds.<ref>[http://www.users.zetnet.co.uk/corncrake/corncrake/cornb146.html A Touch Of Argyll In Norfolk] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090108212607/http://www.users.zetnet.co.uk/corncrake/corncrake/cornb146.html |date=2009-01-08 }} Julia Page in ''The Corncrake'', Colonsay, Scotland " I was intrigued to discover that the common name of lycium halimifolium is the Duke of Argyll's Tea-tree or Teaplant and was keen to discover how this name came about. I succeeded with the help of my friend Craig ( nice Scottish name ) at Kew Gardens Library and a historical Who's Who. Accessed November 2006
</ref>

The plant continues to grow wild in UK [[hedgerows]]. On 15 January 2003, the [[Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs]] launched a project to improve the regulations protecting traditional countryside hedgerows, and specifically mentioned Duke of Argyll's Tea Tree as one of the species to be found growing in hedges located in [[Suffolk]] Sandlings, [[Hadleigh, Suffolk|Hadleigh]], [[Bawdsey]], near [[Ipswich]], and [[Walberswick]].<ref>[http://www.defra.gov.uk/news/2003/030115b.htm Government Launches Consultation On Future Of Legal Protection For Hedgerows] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090720015211/http://www.defra.gov.uk/news/2003/030115b.htm |date=2009-07-20 }} Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs, 15 January 2003. Retrieved 6 September 2006.</ref>

Importation of mature ''Lycium barbarum'' plants into the United Kingdom from most countries outside Europe is illegal, due to the possibility they could be vectors of diseases attacking Solanaceae crops, such as potato or tomato.<ref>Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs, April, 2008. [http://www.defra.gov.uk/news/2008/080430b.htm Prohibited Import of Goji Plants] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080603012504/http://www.defra.gov.uk/news/2008/080430b.htm |date=2008-06-03 }}. April 30, 2008</ref>

===Australia===
''Lycium barbarum'' introduced to [[Australia]] became naturalised in south-eastern coastal and sub-coastal regions, and is regarded as an environmental weed in the states of [[Victoria (Australia)|Victoria]] and [[Tasmania]]. It is often found growing in disturbed sites,  native bushland, and riverbanks, often forming dense thickets along the latter.  It overlaps and is often confused with ''[[Lycium ferocissimum]]'', a similar but spinier species originating from [[Africa]].<ref name=aussie1>Queensland Government (2016), "[https://keyserver.lucidcentral.org/weeds/data/media/Html/lycium_barbarum.htm ''Lycium barbarum'']". Online fact sheet on ''Weeds of Australia'' website. Accessed on 2018-05-04.</ref>

==Chemistry==
[[Phytochemical]]s present in the fruit, root, and other parts of the plants have been studied in some detail.<ref name=potterat>Olivier Potterat (2010): "Goji (''Lycium barbarum'' and ''L. chinense''): Phytochemistry, pharmacology and safety in the perspective of traditional uses and recent popularity".  ''Planta medica'', volume 76, issue 1, pages 7-19.  {{doi|10.1055/s-0029-1186218}}</ref>

The main compounds in the fruit (23% of the dry mass) are [[polysaccharide]]s and [[proteoglycan]]s. [[Carotenoid]] pigments are the second major group, chiefly [[zeaxanthin]] [[palmitic acid|dipalmitate]]. Other detected compounds include [[flavonoid]]s derived from [[myricetin]], [[quercetin]], and [[kaempferol]]; [[hexadecanoic acid]], [[linoleic acid]], and [[myristic acid]]. Other compounds include [[β-sitosterol]], [[scopoletin]], and [[p-coumaric acid]]. The alkaloid [[atropine]], common in plants of the family [[Solanaceae]], is not detectable.<ref name=potterat/>

The compounds present in the roots have been less studied, but they include [[trimethylglycine|betaine]], [[choline]], [[linoleic acid]], and β-sitosterol [79].  Of particular interest are cyclic [[oligopeptide]]s with 8 aminoacid rings.<ref name=potterat/>

The leaves are known to contain the flavonoids quercetin 3-O-[[rutin]]oside-7-O-glucoside, kaempferol 3-O-rutinoside-7-O-glucoside, [[rutin]], [[isoquercitrin]], [[quercetin]], kaempferol [[damascenone]], choline, scopoletin, [[vanillic acid]], [[salicylic acid]], and [[nicotinic acid]].  From the flowers, [[diosgenin]], β-sitosterol, and [[lanosterol]] have been isolated.<ref name=potterat/>
